title: Esther 9:1–19
context: On the thirteenth of Adar, the day the Jews’ enemies hoped to overpower them, “the opposite happened” (9:1). The Jews gather to defend themselves against those who sought their harm, and provincial officials help them out of fear of Mordecai. The text reports the deaths plainly: five hundred men in the citadel of Susa, including Haman’s ten sons (9:6–10); at Esther’s request, a second day in Susa, in which three hundred more men are killed, and the hanging of Haman’s ten sons, who had already been killed (9:13–15); and seventy-five thousand “of those who hated them” in the provinces (9:16). Three times the narrator says that they did not lay their hand on the plunder (9:10, 15, 16), although the decree of 8:11 had allowed it; the text does not explain why. The unit ends by explaining why Jews in the provinces rest and feast on the fourteenth of Adar, and Jews in Susa on the fifteenth (9:17–19). This page describes these events soberly, without endorsing, excusing, or sensationalizing them. Both traditions read the deliverance as shared ground while taking the violence seriously as part of a real and grim history.

verses.text: Now in the twelfth month, which is the month Adar, on the thirteenth day of the month, when the king’s commandment and his decree came near to be put in execution, on the day that the enemies of the Jews hoped to conquer them, (but it turned out that the opposite happened, that the Jews conquered those who hated them),
verses.arminianNotes: On the day the Jews’ enemies hoped to overpower them, “the opposite happened.” Arminian readers note the narrator’s emphasis on reversal. The plans of those who sought the Jews’ destruction fail, and the day of danger becomes a day of deliverance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the great reversal at the center of the book, which many in both traditions attribute to God’s hidden providence, though the text does not name God. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the turning point of the story, without making the silence either a proof or a code.

verses.text: the Jews gathered themselves together in their cities throughout all the provinces of the King Ahasuerus, to lay hands on those who wanted to harm them. No one could withstand them, because the fear of them had fallen on all the people.
verses.arminianNotes: The Jews gather in their cities to lay hands on those who wanted to harm them, and no one can withstand them, because fear of them has fallen on all the people. Arminian readers note that the Jews act in self-defense under the king’s decree. The verse is reported plainly.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read the verse as describing a defensive gathering against those who sought their harm. Shared ground: both traditions describe the events soberly, as the text gives them, without endorsing or excusing the violence that follows.

verses.text: All the princes of the provinces, the local governors, the governors, and those who did the king’s business helped the Jews, because the fear of Mordecai had fallen on them.
verses.arminianNotes: The provincial officials help the Jews because the fear of Mordecai has fallen on them. Arminian readers note that political realities shift with Mordecai’s rise. Officials who might have supported Haman’s decree now side with the Jews.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the change in the officials’ loyalty as part of the reversal. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as explaining why the Jews were able to defend themselves, and both take the narrator’s stated reason, fear of Mordecai, at face value.

verses.text: For Mordecai was great in the king’s house, and his fame went out throughout all the provinces, for the man Mordecai grew greater and greater.
verses.arminianNotes: Mordecai is great in the king’s house, and his fame spreads throughout the provinces. Arminian readers note the rise of a faithful man who once sat at the king’s gate (2:21). His influence now shapes the outcome for his people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Mordecai’s growing greatness as part of the story’s reversal of fortunes, which many readers attribute to hidden providence. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as describing Mordecai’s rise, and both note that the book closes on the same theme (10:2–3).

verses.text: The Jews struck all their enemies with the stroke of the sword, and with slaughter and destruction, and did what they wanted to those who hated them.
verses.arminianNotes: The Jews strike their enemies with the sword and do what they want to those who hate them. Arminian readers read the verse soberly. The narrator reports the violence directly, and they neither celebrate it nor explain it away; it is part of a grim history.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise describe the verse plainly, recognizing that Scripture records events without always commending them. Shared ground: both traditions take the account seriously as history, decline to sensationalize it, and decline to make it a pattern for later conduct.

verses.text: In the citadel of Susa, the Jews killed and destroyed five hundred men.
verses.arminianNotes: In the citadel of Susa, the Jews kill five hundred men. Arminian readers report the number as the text gives it. The fighting reaches the royal city itself, where Haman’s influence had been strongest, and the narrator records the toll without comment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise report the figure plainly and without elaboration. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse soberly as part of the historical account, neither expanding nor minimizing what the text states.

verses.arminianNotes: Parshandatha, Dalphon, and Aspatha are named among those killed. Arminian readers note that these are the first of Haman’s ten sons (9:10). Naming them underlines that Haman’s house comes to an end, as the story has anticipated.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the naming of Haman’s sons and read it as part of the reversal of Haman’s plot. Shared ground: both traditions read the list soberly, as the narrator gives it, without treating the names as a subject for speculation.

verses.arminianNotes: Poratha, Adalia, and Aridatha continue the list of Haman’s sons. Arminian readers read the verse as part of the record of what happened in Susa. The list confirms the end of Haman’s family line, which had shared in his power.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read the names as historical record. Shared ground: both traditions take the verse as part of the sober account of the fighting, and neither builds a theological point on the individual names.

verses.arminianNotes: Parmashta, Arisai, Aridai, and Vaizatha complete the list. Arminian readers note that the narrator takes care to name all ten. The precision of the record reflects the significance of Haman’s house in the story.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the completeness of the list. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as completing the record of Haman’s sons, and both handle it soberly, without sensationalizing their deaths.

verses.text: the ten sons of Haman the son of Hammedatha, the Jews’ enemy, but they didn’t lay their hand on the plunder.
verses.arminianNotes: These are the ten sons of Haman, “the Jews’ enemy,” but they did not lay their hand on the plunder. Arminian readers note the narrator’s statement that the plunder allowed in 8:11 was not taken. The text records it without explaining the reason.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the statement and its repetition in 9:15–16, without supplying a motive the text does not give. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as recording the end of Haman’s house and the restraint concerning plunder, exactly as the text states it.

verses.text: On that day, the number of those who were slain in the citadel of Susa was brought before the king.
verses.arminianNotes: The number of those killed in Susa is brought before the king that day. Arminian readers note that the king is kept informed. The report shows that the events took place under royal authority, not as unchecked disorder.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read the verse as part of the official record of the day. Shared ground: both traditions read it as narrative transition to the king’s conversation with Esther, with no doctrinal question raised.

verses.text: The king said to Esther the queen, “The Jews have slain and destroyed five hundred men in the citadel of Susa, including the ten sons of Haman; what then have they done in the rest of the king’s provinces! Now what is your petition? It shall be granted you. What is your further request? It shall be done.”
verses.arminianNotes: The king tells Esther what has happened in Susa and asks what more she wants. Arminian readers note the king’s readiness to grant further requests. His question sets up Esther’s petition for a second day in Susa.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the king’s continued favor toward Esther. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as reporting the king’s words plainly, including the numbers he cites, without adding commentary on his attitude beyond what the text shows.

verses.text: Then Esther said, “If it pleases the king, let it be granted to the Jews who are in Susa to do tomorrow also according to today’s decree, and let Haman’s ten sons be hanged on the gallows.”
verses.arminianNotes: Esther asks that the Jews in Susa be allowed to act again the next day, and that Haman’s ten sons be hanged. Arminian readers report her request soberly. The text does not explain her reasons, and they do not supply motives beyond what is written.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise describe the request plainly, without endorsing or condemning it beyond the narrator’s own presentation. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a difficult part of the record, and both decline to speculate about Esther’s inner reasoning.

verses.text: The king commanded this to be done. A decree was given out in Susa; and they hanged Haman’s ten sons.
verses.arminianNotes: The king commands it, a decree is issued in Susa, and Haman’s ten sons are hanged. Arminian readers note that the sons had already been killed (9:10), so the hanging is a public display. The text reports it without further comment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read the verse as describing a public act carried out under royal decree. Shared ground: both traditions describe it soberly, as the text gives it, and both see it as the final end of Haman’s house in the narrative.

verses.text: The Jews who were in Susa gathered themselves together on the fourteenth day also of the month Adar, and killed three hundred men in Susa; but they didn’t lay their hand on the plunder.
verses.arminianNotes: On the fourteenth of Adar the Jews in Susa kill three hundred men, but they do not lay their hand on the plunder. Arminian readers report the number as given and note the second statement about the plunder, recorded without explanation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise report the figure and the restraint as the text states them. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse soberly as part of the historical account, neither expanding nor softening it, and neither supplying a reason for the restraint.

verses.text: The other Jews who were in the king’s provinces gathered themselves together, defended their lives, had rest from their enemies, and killed seventy-five thousand of those who hated them; but they didn’t lay their hand on the plunder.
verses.arminianNotes: The Jews in the provinces defend their lives, have rest from their enemies, and kill seventy-five thousand of those who hated them, but do not take plunder. Arminian readers report the figure as given and note the narrator’s description of the dead as those who hated them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise report the number and the third statement about plunder exactly as the text gives them. Shared ground: both traditions take the verse seriously as part of a grim history, without sensationalizing it, sanitizing it, or turning it into a modern political argument.

verses.text: This was done on the thirteenth day of the month Adar; and on the fourteenth day of that month they rested and made it a day of feasting and gladness.
verses.arminianNotes: This happens on the thirteenth of Adar, and on the fourteenth they rest and make it a day of feasting and gladness. Arminian readers note that the narrative moves from fighting to rest. The celebration marks relief from a threat of destruction.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the movement from danger to rest and joy. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as explaining the origin of the feast day in the provinces, and both see rest from enemies as the fitting end of the threat that hung over the Jews.

verses.text: But the Jews who were in Susa assembled together on the thirteenth and on the fourteenth days of the month; and on the fifteenth day of that month, they rested, and made it a day of feasting and gladness.
verses.arminianNotes: The Jews in Susa act on the thirteenth and fourteenth and rest on the fifteenth with feasting and gladness. Arminian readers note that the narrator explains why Susa’s observance differs from that of the provinces. The difference arises from the history itself.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read the verse as explaining the two dates of the festival. Shared ground: both traditions read it as a historical explanation of Purim’s observance, with no doctrinal question raised by the difference in dates.

verses.text: Therefore the Jews of the villages, who live in the unwalled towns, make the fourteenth day of the month Adar a day of gladness and feasting, a holiday, and a day of sending presents of food to one another.
verses.arminianNotes: The Jews of the villages and unwalled towns keep the fourteenth as a day of gladness, feasting, holiday, and sending food to one another. Arminian readers note that joy is shared through generosity. The celebration builds community.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the giving of food as a fitting expression of thanksgiving. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as describing a joyful and generous custom that grew from deliverance, and both affirm that remembering rescue with gladness is right.
